sources.title: Vikram Sarabhai (Q325470), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-18): English label 'Vikram Sarabhai', description 'father of Indian space programme (1919-1971)', Korean label 비크람 사라바이, born 1919-08-12, died 1971-12-30, a human, citizen of India. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vikram Sarabhai' (read in full, updated October 2026). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Indian physicist and industrialist who initiated space research and helped develop nuclear power in India; born into a family of industrialists; Cambridge tripos 1940; cosmic-ray research under C. V. Raman at the Indian Institute of Science; doctorate 1947; founded the Physical Research Laboratory in Ahmedabad; founded the Ahmedabad Textile Industry's Research Association in 1947 and ran it until 1956; set up the Indian Institute of Management, Ahmedabad (1962); established the Indian National Committee for Space Research in 1962 (later ISRO) and the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station; chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission after Homi Bhabha's death in 1966; argued for space applications as 'levers of development' and for satellite education of remote villages; Padma Bhushan 1966, Padma Vibhushan 1972. Short reference article, admiring.

Indian Space Research Organisation, 'Dr. Vikram Ambalal Sarabhai (1963-1971)', former-chairman page (read in full). INSTITUTIONAL SOURCE (self-interested): says that after returning from Cambridge in 1947 he persuaded charitable trusts controlled by his family and friends to endow a research institution in Ahmedabad, founding the Physical Research Laboratory on 11 November 1947 at 28; lists the institutions he founded or helped found (the Physical Research Laboratory, the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad with other Ahmedabad industrialists, the Community Science Centre, the Darpan Academy for Performing Arts with his wife, the Space Applications Centre and others); gives the first rocket launch from Thumba on 21 November 1963, his 1966 dialogue with NASA that led to the satellite television experiment of 1975-76, and his 'second to none in the application of advanced technologies to the real problems of man and society' statement. Agency's own biography of its founder.

Indian Institute of Science, 'Dr. Vikram Sarabhai's 100th Birth Anniversary' (page read; the page names Amrita Shah's biography 'Vikram Sarabhai: A Life' as its source). At the institute in 1940 under C. V. Raman, who introduced his first paper by saying he had been brought up 'with a silver spoon in his mouth' and had faith that he would contribute much; Sarabhai later helped Raman obtain funds from Ahmedabad industrialists; his friendship with Homi Bhabha, with whom he shared a love of arts and culture; the 1947 founding of the Physical Research Laboratory, the 1962 chairmanship of the national space committee and the choice of Thumba; his family businesses, the textile research association, the market-research firm Operations Research Group, a short-lived weight-loss product, and help in setting up other institutions. Institutional centenary tribute drawn from a biography; admiring.

Haitian Ma, 'Leapfrogging India: Vikram Sarabhai and the developmental promise of geocentric spaceflight', The British Journal for the History of Science 58 (2025), pp. 261-280 (open-access article; full text read). INDEPENDENT, PARTLY CRITICAL SCHOLARSHIP on how his public image was built: records his 1962 mediation of the agreement with NASA for rockets at Thumba, his chairmanship of the UN outer-space committee, the 16 October 1966 All India Radio talk in which he first used the term 'leap-frog' for space and development, the 1970 ten-year plan for atomic energy and space research and the press criticism that called it indiscreet and costly, the 1968 memorandum with NASA for the satellite instructional television experiment, and his appointment to head the atomic energy department in 1966; cites historians who call his development thinking technocratic and elitist and a nuclear colleague (Homi Sethna) who called him a sheltered idealist, and notes that Amrita Shah reads his reticence on the nuclear question as restraint and patience; argues that his persona was mostly built after his death. Peer-reviewed article that also warns of a hagiographical tone in many accounts.

A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, address 'Interaction with Students', Office of the President of India website (page read). COLLEAGUE TESTIMONY, retrospective: Kalam, who worked in the 1960s at the Thumba church that became the rocket station, recalls Sarabhai and Homi Bhabha searching for an equatorial site, Sarabhai meeting politicians and officials without success, being sent in 1962 to the Bishop of Trivandrum, and the bishop's Sunday address to his congregation that ended in a chorus of 'Amen' for giving up the church and bishop's house for space research; the church then served as his design centre and the bishop's house as the scientists' place. Speech by a later president recalling an event four decades earlier; admiring of both men.

Live History India, 'Vikram Sarabhai and India's Space Odyssey' (Aditi Shah, 18 May 2019; page read): popular article saying he attended the 1957-58 International Geophysical Year as India's representative when Sputnik was launched, that the space programme was meant to serve education, weather and disaster warning and village television, that he selected young engineers from the Physical Research Laboratory and the atomic energy department (among them A. P. J. Abdul Kalam and R. Aravamudan) to train at NASA, that he persuaded the church's bishop to give up the Thumba site, that equipment for the 1963 launch was largely loaned or given by the United States, the UK and West Germany (quoting Aravamudan), and that he helped set up 42 institutions. Popular retelling that depends on ISRO's biography and on memoirs; contains a death-date slip (30 November for 30 December).

The Tribune (Chandigarh), 'Vikram Sarabhai: Father of India's space programme' (Time Capsule feature by Sanjay Khurana, updated 30 December 2024; page read): newspaper retelling that he co-founded the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad in 1961 (Britannica says 1962), founded the Community Science Centre to popularise science education, advocated international partnership in space and peaceful use, and that the first Indian satellite Aryabhata flew in 1975. Short newspaper feature drawing on the agency's account; used only for consistency of dates.

NASA Headquarters photo record GPN-2002-000081 (NASA image 69-H-1540), 'Dr. Vikram Sarabhai and Dr. Paine Sign a Satellite Agreement', dated 18 September 1969 (archived copy of NASA's Great Images in NASA database page, read; creator NASA, large file 2752 x 2245): caption names Vikram A. Sarabhai (left), chairman of the Indian Space Research Organization and head of India's Department of Atomic Energy, and NASA Administrator Thomas O. Paine signing an agreement for an experiment using a space satellite to bring instructional television programmes to Indian villages; the satellite (ATS-6) became available to India's space organisation on 1 August 1975 for one year. Holder photo record, used for the 1969 agreement and for the portrait.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_sarabhai_isro, src_sarabhai_britannica, src_sarabhai_iisc, src_sarabhai_bjhs, src_sarabhai_lhi | 1947-1969 | agency biography, reference article, institute tribute, scholarly article, popular article] On returning from Cambridge in 1947 he persuaded trusts controlled by his family and friends to fund a research institute and founded the Physical Research Laboratory at 28 (ISRO, IISc); the same year he founded the Ahmedabad Textile Industry's Research Association (Britannica), later the management institute (1961-62, with other industrialists), the national space committee in 1962 and the equatorial rocket station at Thumba, and by one popular count 42 institutions (Live History India). Ma's article credits his mediation of the NASA agreement for the rocket launch. CONCENTRATION: the institution list is mostly the agency's own biography and Ma warns of a hagiographical tone; the family's wealth and Bhabha's backing were enabling conditions, and he shared the founding of several bodies. Lowered from 78 / 0.62 to 74 / 0.58.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: [src_sarabhai_lhi, src_sarabhai_isro, src_sarabhai_kalam, src_sarabhai_iisc | 1957-1966 | popular article, agency biography, colleague testimony, institute tribute] Live History India says that at the 1957-58 Geophysical Year, where Sputnik was launched, he began to argue for an Indian space programme; the agency's page and the institute tribute describe him turning cosmic-ray work into space research and, after dialogue with NASA in 1966, a satellite television experiment; Kalam recalls the search for an equatorial site that settled on Thumba. The pattern of spotting a new field and a way to fund it is repeated, but the reasoning behind each choice comes largely from the agency and later tributes. CONCENTRATION: motives rest on the agency's biography and popular retelling; lowered from 70 / 0.54 to 66 / 0.50.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_sarabhai_isro, src_sarabhai_iisc, src_sarabhai_kalam, src_sarabhai_bjhs | 1947-1966 | agency biography, institute tribute, colleague testimony, scholarly article] He persuaded family and friends' trusts to fund the Physical Research Laboratory and, per the agency, persuaded the government of the case for a space programme after Sputnik; he helped Raman raise funds from Ahmedabad industrialists (IISc); Kalam recalls the 1962 meeting at which the Bishop of Trivandrum agreed to give up the Thumba church; Ma credits his mediation of the NASA rocket agreement and his UN committee roles. CONCENTRATION: the bishop episode is a single event retold by Kalam and popular articles, and the first two claims come from the agency; lowered from 72 / 0.56 to 68 / 0.52.

collaboration.rationale: [src_sarabhai_iisc, src_sarabhai_bjhs, src_sarabhai_lhi, src_sarabhai_kalam | 1940-1969 | institute tribute, scholarly article, popular article, colleague testimony] The institute tribute describes a long friendship and professional partnership with Homi Bhabha; Ma records agreements with NASA and the Soviet hydro-meteorological service and a network of international contacts; Live History India describes him choosing young engineers for NASA training, and Kalam recalls the team working at the Thumba church. How he worked with others day to day is little described, and Ma notes colleagues in the atomic energy sector saw him as an idealist outside their line. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.50 to 62 / 0.46 (relabelled inference) because partnerships are documented by agreements and tributes, not by an account of how work was shared.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_sarabhai_isro, src_sarabhai_britannica, src_sarabhai_bjhs, src_sarabhai_lhi | 1962-1971 | agency biography, reference article, scholarly article, popular article] He argued that space activities in a developing country should be applied to the real problems of people (the 'second to none in the application of advanced technologies' statement, repeated by the agency and popular articles), planned satellite education for villages (Britannica, Ma), founded a community science centre and other civic institutions, and in 1966 coined the 'leap-frog' line on air. Ma cites historians who find his development thinking technocratic and elitist and little tied to rural needs, so the intent is documented while the results are disputed. CONCENTRATION: the headline statement is one quotation reported by several outlets; lowered from 78 / 0.62 to 72 / 0.54.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_sarabhai_britannica, src_sarabhai_isro, src_sarabhai_bjhs, src_sarabhai_lhi | 1947-1971 | reference article, agency biography, scholarly article, popular article] He headed the Physical Research Laboratory, the national space committee, the atomic energy department and the Atomic Energy Commission, and, per Live History India, chose the first group of young rocket engineers; Ma notes a crisis of authority in the atomic sector in his last years and colleagues who found him too idealistic. Positions are documented; the sources say little about how he led people. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.50 to 62 / 0.46 (relabelled inference) because the evidence is a record of offices held, not described leadership behaviour.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_sarabhai_britannica, src_sarabhai_iisc, src_sarabhai_isro, src_sarabhai_lhi | 1940-1971 | reference article, institute tribute, agency biography, popular article] Beyond cosmic-ray physics he ran family firms, founded a textile research association and a market-research firm, helped found a management institute, a community science centre and a performing-arts academy with his wife, and led atomic energy and space programmes (Britannica, IISc, ISRO). The range is broad and documented across several sources, though the commercial ventures are mostly from one biography-based tribute. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.56 to 70 / 0.52 because the business and arts items rest mainly on one biography-derived page and the agency's list.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_sarabhai_kalam, src_sarabhai_lhi, src_sarabhai_bjhs, src_sarabhai_isro | 1947-1967 | colleague testimony, popular article, scholarly article, agency biography] He started the research laboratory in his family's house with family-controlled trusts' money (Live History India, ISRO), obtained a church and bishop's house for the first launch site (Kalam), and secured rockets and equipment from the United States, the Soviet Union and others (Ma; an engineer's memoir quoted by Live History India says much came on loan or as gifts). Means were largely lent by foreign partners and family wealth, so the sources describe access more than improvisation. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.52 to 64 / 0.48 (relabelled inference) because family wealth and foreign donors supplied most of the means.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_sarabhai_iisc, src_sarabhai_isro | 1940s-1971 | institute tribute, agency biography] The institute tribute says he and Homi Bhabha bonded over a love of arts and culture, and the agency lists the Darpan Academy for Performing Arts, which he founded with his wife, among his institutions. Documented interest and patronage; the sources say nothing about his own taste or creative practice.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_sarabhai_bjhs, src_sarabhai_isro | 1966-1970 | scholarly article, agency biography] Ma records his 1969 call for a five- to ten-year national objective and the 1970 ten-year plan for atomic energy and space research (satellite television, synchronous satellites), which the press called indiscreet and too costly; the agency records the 1966 NASA dialogue that led to the satellite television experiment. A documented long-range plan, partly criticised as unrealistic, so impact is dual-edged.

portrait.source: Photograph of Vikram A. Sarabhai (seated left) with NASA Administrator Thomas O. Paine signing an agreement for a satellite instructional-television experiment, NASA Headquarters photo 69-H-1540 (GRIN database number GPN-2002-000081), dated 18 September 1969, creator NASA; the archived NASA record (large file 2752 x 2245) was read, and the image was taken from the Wikimedia Commons copy of that file (served at 1920 x 1566). The file is a crop of Sarabhai alone (head, shoulders and pen hand) converted to greyscale and resized to 911 x 1000, which is a downscale of the native crop (1130 x 1240 in the served file): no upscaling.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (Stage B) / LEAD SURVIVED with a larger source. Lead was NASA photo GPN-2002-000081 as cropped on Commons 'Vikram Sarabhai.jpg' (only 353 x 478). The full file exists on Commons (2752 x 2245; 1920 x 1566 served) and the original NASA record was read through an archived copy of NASA's GRIN database page (the live GRIN link is dead and NASA's image API has no entry; the Wayback copy's rights-notice link then hit a Wayback rate-limit block, recorded as a bot wall, not bypassed): NASA HQ image 69-H-1540, dated 09/18/1969, creator NASA, caption naming Sarabhai (left) and Administrator Paine, large file 2752 x 2245 matching Commons. Rights basis: US-government (NASA) photograph; NASA's current media guidelines (read) say NASA content is generally not subject to copyright and may be used with acknowledgement and no implied endorsement; no copyright notice found on the record. Holder contradiction: the caption text on Commons and in the NASA record adds a 1974-75 satellite paragraph that post-dates the 1969 photograph (background, not about the date); the NASA record says the instructional experiment would reach 'some 5,000' villages whereas a 2025 scholarly article says about 400 were selected, so no village count is used. Identity: caption-only (no lettering in the image) but the man on the left matches the ISRO official portrait of Sarabhai (compared by eye). The second man is Paine. KIND likeness (a documented 1969 photograph). Not used: Flickr 1951 photograph (nat507, CC BY 2.0, 314 x 500; Flickr page not opened) and the ISRO official portrait (GODL-India; undated). Crop of a two-person image: Paine is removed by the crop. IDENTITY: QID Q325470 verified live 2026-11-18 (label 'Vikram Sarabhai', description 'father of Indian space programme (1919-1971)', ko 비크람 사라바이, born 1919-08-12, died 1971-12-30, human, citizen of India). ATTRIBUTION: attributable (dated institutions, a mainstream biography, scholarly work). INHERITED ADVANTAGE: born to a wealthy industrial family whose trusts funded his first institute; the profile scores behaviour (persuading, founding, planning), not wealth, and several rows are lowered for this.
